analysis.one_liner: Bans hiring contracts that silence workers about workplace harassment and makes harassment settlements nondeductible for employers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 98 cosponsors, including 2 Republicans, but was never taken up by any of the six committees it was sent to and died without a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The EMPOWER Act would make it illegal for employers to require workers or job applicants to sign nondisclosure or nondisparagement agreements covering workplace or sexual harassment as a condition of a job. It would let workers report harassment to government agencies or courts regardless of any agreement they signed. It would also require public companies to report their harassment settlement counts and payments to the SEC, take away the tax deduction employers currently get for harassment judgments and legal fees, make harassment settlement payments tax-free for the workers who receive them, and fund EEOC training programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants — including temps, contractors, interns, and federal and congressional employees — who would no longer be bound by contract clauses that keep them quiet about harassment. Workers receiving harassment settlements would pay no income tax on those payments, and people winning back pay after discrimination would avoid a tax penalty from a one-year income spike.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits employers from entering into, or trying to enforce, employment contracts containing nondisparagement or nondisclosure clauses covering workplace or sexual harassment, and from unilaterally putting such a clause in a separation agreement [S2] [S3].
Preserves every worker's right to report harassment to the EEOC, other federal agencies, state fair employment agencies, law enforcement, or federal court, regardless of anything they signed [S3].

Requires public companies to disclose to the SEC, over the most recent five years, the number and dollar total of harassment settlements and judgments, plus whether three or more settlements involved the same individual [S2] [S3].

Denies employers the federal tax deduction for harassment judgments, litigation expenses, and insurance covering harassment claims, while excluding harassment settlement and judgment amounts from workers' taxable income and allowing income averaging for back pay [S2] [S3].

Directs the EEOC to develop workplace training and public education about harassment, including bystander intervention, taking effect only in years it receives at least $1.5 million in appropriations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers lose the ability to buy silence with NDAs at hire, lose a tax deduction for harassment judgments and defense costs, and must publicly report settlement counts and totals. Companies with repeated harassment settlements would face reputational and shareholder scrutiny, and the Treasury forgoes tax revenue on settlement payments made tax-free to workers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers with harassment NDAs and settlements

drawbacks.text: The bill still allows nondisclosure clauses in settlement or separation agreements resolving claims that arose before the agreement, so harassment victims who take a settlement can still be paid for silence — the ban covers only hiring-time contracts and one-sided clauses [S2] [S3].

Denying deductions for harassment judgments and related insurance raises employers' after-tax cost of losing harassment lawsuits; supporters intend this as a deterrent, but employers facing litigation would bear higher costs regardless of merit [S3].

Making settlement payments tax-free and requiring public disclosure of settlement counts imposes a revenue cost on the Treasury and new SEC reporting requirements on public companies, with the training programs dependent on a dedicated $1.5 million annual appropriation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core benefit — workers can no longer be contractually gagged about harassment before they even get the job — directly addresses a practice widely criticized after #MeToo and costs employers only the ability to buy that silence. The tax provisions cut both ways: they raise the price of losing a harassment suit and give workers tax-free recovery, at a revenue cost to Treasury. The main honest limitation is that it does not touch NDAs in negotiated settlements, so the most common way victims are paid for silence remains legal.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to six House committees on the day it was introduced, none of which ever took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced November 3, 2021 by Rep. Lois Frankel with 65 original cosponsors, and referred the same day to the committees on Education and Labor, Ways and Means, Judiciary, House Administration, Oversight and Reform, and Financial Services [S1] [S3] [S5].
It gathered 98 cosponsors, 96 Democrats and 2 Republicans, including senior members who chaired or sat on the very committees it was referred to [S4].
No committee held a markup or hearing, no version was ever reported out, and the House never voted on it; the referral was the bill's last action [S5].

The Congress ended January 3, 2023, killing the bill; the broader problem of harassment NDAs was addressed only partially by the separate Speak Out Act, enacted in late 2022, which barred pre-dispute NDAs for sexual harassment claims but left the SEC-disclosure and tax provisions unadopted [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off: they keep the right to require NDAs covering harassment at hire, keep the tax deduction for harassment judgments and defense costs, and face no SEC settlement-disclosure requirement. Workers gained nothing from this bill.

for.name: Lois Frankel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: 98 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: 96 Democrats and 2 Republicans cosponsored the bill, signaling enough support to pass the House had it reached the floor.

against.name: House committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the six committees of referral, including Education and Labor and Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for markup, hearing, or a vote in any of the six committees; the bill's last recorded action was the referral itself.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was almost entirely Democratic — 96 of 98 cosponsors — with only 2 Republicans (Reps. Katko and Fitzpatrick, among the original cosponsors) supporting it, and no House vote ever occurred [S3] [S4].

industries.note: They would lose the ability to condition jobs on NDAs covering harassment, lose the tax deduction for harassment judgments and defense insurance, and would have to report settlement counts and totals to the SEC, subjecting repeat offenders to public scrutiny. Their interest in keeping these tools runs against workers' ability to speak.

industries.industry: Employment-law defense firms and insurers covering harassment liability
industries.note: The bill denies deductions for litigation expenses and for insurance covering harassment claims, raising the cost of defending and insuring against harassment suits. Their revenue depends on the volume and cost of harassment litigation.
